title: A partition observable separates its mean from its typical and frozen regimes
claim: The squared-modulus short-window integral is a positive coarse-graining of the local zeta landscape: its known global mean can coexist with a different typical scale if rare windows dominate, while the beta-dependent free-energy response tests that domination across a family of exponents rather than at one mean value.
historical_or_program_relation: The freezing program supplies a distributional response-curve conjecture for the same kind of local partition mass whose typical size is isolated as an analytic question in the short-window second-moment program.
limits: The short-window source does not establish a mean/typical gap or a tail mechanism. The reported freezing plateau is numerical, uses lower-order arithmetic renormalization, and is explicitly a proposed model rather than a theorem for zeta.

title: Upper and lower maximum bounds use opposite sides of multiscale path geometry
claim: Both maximum programs replace pointwise search by a path through prime scales, but in opposite directions: Cauchy localization, smooth-factor thresholds, and optimized high moments make upper-barrier failure rare, whereas matched-variance prime blocks, a spatial grid, and Paley-Zygmund produce a point whose blocks are simultaneously high.
historical_or_program_relation: Together the programs decompose a local-maximum problem into an analytic transfer to prime blocks and a probability problem on correlated multiscale paths, with barrier estimates for the upper direction and second-moment abundance for the lower direction.
limits: The arguments use different approximations, events, parameter ranges, and inequality directions. They do not identify an exact common random field, prove the FHK limiting law, or convert the typical-window lower bound into a global-maximum result.

title: Two cutoff factorizations preserve different invariants
claim: A smooth/rough factorization of a shortened approximate-functional-equation polynomial preserves zeta only in a quantified mean-square sense, while the smoothed hybrid Euler-Hadamard factorization moves mass between prime and nearby-zero factors as its cutoff changes while preserving their product. In both cases the cutoff is part of the representation and records what the separated factors forget.
historical_or_program_relation: The two programs turn zeta into coupled factors for different purposes: coefficient-scale independence for maximum estimates versus an explicit prime/zero division that restores arithmetic to a characteristic-polynomial model.
limits: The smooth/rough factors are finite Dirichlet polynomials with an L2 error and are not the hybrid prime and zero factors. The cutoff-compensation evidence includes a representation-sensitivity visualization and does not justify termwise identification or statistical independence of either pair.

title: GCD optimization and positive convolution separate resonator design from analytic transfer
claim: The GCD quadratic form designs coefficients with many favorable multiplicative ratios, while the positive Dirichlet-series lemma and compact-frequency kernel convert approximate relations of the form km approximately n into a localized lower bound. Thus multiplicative-ratio geometry is the interface between arithmetic support optimization and analytic amplification.
historical_or_program_relation: One program supplies a near-extremal multiplicative support and its compressed ratio geometry; the other abstracts the positivity and smoothing mechanism that lets a finite favorable coefficient block survive time averaging and localization.
limits: The GCD construction and the positive-convolution theorem have distinct support, smoothing, and interval budgets. Their combination does not prove an optimal zeta maximum, transfer the GCD constant automatically, or apply when the projected Dirichlet coefficients have uncontrolled signs.

title: Signed projections obstruct the monotone GCD-resonance route
claim: The GCD upper bound limits a positive-coefficient resonance architecture, but argument extremes introduce a different obstruction: imaginary projection of the smoothed logarithm produces signed prime coefficients and an explicit off-line-zero correction, while the Cauchy bridge from log modulus to S1 has a signed kernel. Positivity can no longer certify that discarding terms improves a one-sided lower bound.
historical_or_program_relation: Tracing both methods backward distinguishes an arithmetic capacity ceiling from a representation-induced sign barrier; improving smoothing inside the former architecture does not remove the latter.
limits: This is a method-specific obstruction, not an impossibility theorem for extreme values of S or S1. The zero correction and conditional assumptions must remain explicit, and an absolute-value conclusion for S cannot be promoted to a one-sided conclusion for S1.

title: Continuation before specialization keeps boundary claims auditable
claim: Both analyses construct an auxiliary analytic object on a domain where two representations overlap and only then take a boundary operation: derivative extraction recovers zeta coefficients from the ladder-height germ, whereas a coupled two-variable specialization converts a continued identity into a mean-square formula. A finite cutoff is separately required when a boundedly convergent Voronoi series meets an improper integral.
historical_or_program_relation: The shared proof discipline is continuation before specialization, supplemented by explicit order-of-limits control when integration and infinite expansion interact.
limits: The auxiliary functions, domains, and boundary operations are different, so this is not a common theorem. Analytic continuation does not supply a probabilistic meaning at nonpositive drift, and it does not by itself license termwise integration or remove the mean-square convergence boundary.

title: Higher moments replace a controlled divisor oscillation by stratified divisor correlations
claim: For the second moment, an Atkinson-type formula and full-versus-truncated Voronoi expansions turn the error into controlled oscillatory generalized-divisor terms. Expanding higher critical-line moments instead exposes shifted additive divisor correlations, and longer polynomials reveal distinct rational-direction strata that can contribute main terms rather than errors.
historical_or_program_relation: The transition from the explicit second-moment formula to the higher-moment divisor-correlation program marks a concrete increase in proof burden: one oscillatory representation is no longer enough, because off-diagonal correlation geometry must be resolved stratum by stratum.
limits: The second-moment truncation and saddle machinery do not estimate the higher shifted correlations. The random-matrix or swap recipe is a target for the divisor program, not a theorem imported into it, and the rational strata do not establish the full zeta-moment conjecture without analytic error control.

title: Cutoffs, Fourier identities, and nonnegativity audit formal moment expansions
claim: Two moment calculations expose different failures of formal expansion. The mean-square proof repairs an invalid infinite sum-improper integral exchange by cutting the integral before substitution, while a long Dirichlet polynomial reproduces the second moment only after a functional-equation Fourier identity accounts for off-diagonal mass; negative predictions for higher moments then falsify a heuristic missing correlation classes.
historical_or_program_relation: The established finite-cut repair and the long-polynomial diagnostic both make representation validity depend on an explicit certificate—uniform limit control in one case and a Fourier compatibility identity plus the nonnegativity invariant in the other.
limits: The repairs address different analytic failures. Nonnegativity detects that the higher-moment heuristic is incomplete but does not identify or prove the missing terms, and the verified second-moment Fourier identity does not validate the corresponding higher-moment extrapolation.

title: Zero statistics and higher moments meet different shifted arithmetic correlations
claim: Past their diagonal ranges, both zero-pair statistics and zeta moments reduce analytic questions to translation correlations of arithmetic coefficients: pair correlation asks for shifted von Mangoldt products Lambda(n)Lambda(n+h), while the sixth-moment route asks for shifted correlations of divisor coefficients arising from zeta cubed.
historical_or_program_relation: Montgomery's long-polynomial obstruction and the later near-diagonal zero-density calculation isolate the shifted-prime statistic; the higher-moment program exhibits the analogous but distinct additive-divisor bottleneck.
limits: Von Mangoldt and divisor correlations have different weights, shift ranges, smoothing, and conjectural inputs. Hardy-Littlewood averaging, random-matrix agreement, or a delta-method recipe in one setting cannot be imported as a theorem in the other.

title: Moment constants factor into arithmetic data and a density-calibrated geometric model
claim: Matching matrix size to local zero density lets unitary characteristic-polynomial moments predict a geometric factor, but zeta moments retain a separate Euler-product arithmetic factor. For truncated pseudomoments, a substochastic-polytope volume is an exact shared geometric invariant of the zeta polynomial and truncated unitary model, while the zeta side alone keeps the local arithmetic factor.
historical_or_program_relation: The random-matrix program first explains missing combinatorial constants after arithmetic is factored out; the pseudomoment calculation refines that analogy by exhibiting a concrete polytope shared by two truncated representations.
limits: The shared polytope concerns truncated models and does not establish the full zeta moment asymptotic. Density matching and agreement at known low moments support but do not prove universality, and replacing pairwise zeta factors by poles still needs analytic error estimates.

title: Tail shape changes when moment order exhausts the analytic scale budget
claim: High moments convert coefficient variance into level-set bounds only while the associated Dirichlet polynomial fits the averaging interval. Optimizing the admissible moment order yields different moderate and extreme tail shapes, and in a multiscale maximum proof the same optimization must also pay the entropy of all candidate locations and prime blocks.
historical_or_program_relation: The large-value and short-interval moment methods supply the scale-dependent moment budget; the barrier method adds the combinatorial union over a path, explaining why pointwise Gaussian intuition alone is insufficient for maxima.
limits: The sources use different hypotheses, thresholds, intervals, and observables, so no single tail formula is asserted across them. The quadratic and V log V regimes are source-specific bounds, and a barrier estimate is not an exact extreme-value distribution.

title: The averaging measure changes both diagonalization and the observed family law
claim: Changing the ensemble changes more than the available orthogonality relation: character averaging can make prime squares survive and shift the Gaussian center, while a trace-formula weight changes the probability measure itself and can make low-zero statistics appear inconsistent with the unweighted symmetry prediction.
historical_or_program_relation: The family-moment analysis shows how arithmetic terms determine centering after diagonalization; the trace-formula example shows that even a correct representation-theoretic symmetry type can be obscured when the analytically accessible weighted family is not the desired counting family.
limits: The examples involve different families and weights and do not assert a common numerical correction. GRH upper frequencies are only compatible with the random-matrix predictions, and weighted low-zero density cannot by itself identify or refute the unweighted symmetry type.

title: Exact probabilistic coefficients and freezing heuristics have different interfaces to zeta
claim: Probability enters zeta analysis in two noninterchangeable ways: a continued Gaussian-walk ladder-height function has an exact Taylor coefficient identified with zeta(1/2), whereas the log-correlated partition model proposes a distributional law for a field of critical-line values and tests it through a renormalized free-energy curve.
historical_or_program_relation: The ladder-height identity is an exact coefficient bridge built through renewal and Wiener-Hopf analysis; freezing is an ensemble-level explanatory program for extremes. Keeping those interfaces separate prevents a probabilistic vocabulary match from being treated as mathematical transfer.
limits: The exact coefficient identity does not connect ladder heights to the log-correlated field or give a probabilistic meaning to the continued function at nonpositive drift. The freezing curve is numerical and conjectural for zeta, so it cannot be used to infer the ladder identity or an extreme-value theorem.
